Caldron
KAWL-drun
noun
From the Old French caudron, through Latin caldarium, a hot bath or boiling vessel, from calidus, hot; hence a great pot for seething flesh — a temple vessel, and a prophet’s figure for a city under judgment.

Biblical Definition

A caldron is a great boiling pot for seething flesh. It was a vessel of the sanctuary — the fleshhook was struck into “the pan, or kettle, or caldron, or pot” at Shiloh (1Sa 2:14), the caldrons of brass were carried away by the Chaldeans when the temple was stripped (Jer 52:18), and Josiah’s passover offerings were sod in pots and caldrons and pans (2Ch 35:13). But the word’s doctrinal weight is in Ezekiel. The princes of Jerusalem, secure behind their walls after the first deportation, had a proverb: “It is not near; let us build houses: this city is the caldron, and we be the flesh” (Eze 11:3). Their meaning was comfortable — the walls are the iron pot, we are the choice meat inside, protected; judgment falls on the exiles outside, not on us. The LORD takes their own figure and turns it against them. Yes, He says, there is flesh in this caldron: “Your slain whom ye have laid in the midst of it, they are the flesh, and this city is the caldron: but I will bring you forth out of the midst of it” (Eze 11:7). The men they had murdered are the meat; the murderers will be dragged out of the pot to be judged in the border of Israel by the sword they did not fear (Eze 11:10-11). Ezekiel 24 completes it: the caldron is set on the fire with its scum still in it, and the fire is heaped until the very brass burns.

Webster 1828 Definition

A large kettle or boiler for seething flesh; in Ezekiel, the false proverb of a city that thought its walls made it safe.

CALDRON, a large kettle or boiler, of copper or other metal, for boiling flesh or other things.

Old French caudron, Latin caldarium, from calidus, hot.

A vessel of the sanctuary service (1Sa 2:14; 2Ch 35:13; Jer 52:18).

The proverb of Jerusalem: this city is the caldron, and we be the flesh (Eze 11:3).

The LORD’s answer: the slain are the flesh, and the murderers shall be brought forth (Eze 11:7,11).

Key Scripture

Eze 11:3 — "Which say, It is not near; let us build houses: this city is the caldron, and we be the flesh."

Eze 11:7 — "Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Your slain whom ye have laid in the midst of it, they are the flesh, and this city is the caldron: but I will bring you forth out of the midst of it."

Eze 11:11 — "This city shall not be your caldron, neither shall ye be the flesh in the midst thereof; but I will judge you in the border of Israel:"

Mic 3:3 — "Who also eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them; and they break their bones, and chop them in pieces, as for the pot, and as flesh within the caldron."

Modern Corruption

The caldron proverb is carnal security in three clauses — it is not near, let us build houses, we are the safe ones — and it is spoken in churches still.

expand to see more

The live misuse is presumption, and Ezekiel gives its exact liturgy. It is not near — judgment is postponed indefinitely, the warnings belong to another generation, the prophets are alarmists. Let us build houses — therefore invest in the present order as though it were permanent. This city is the caldron, and we be the flesh — and we are the insiders, the chosen, the protected, whatever we do. That last clause is the deadly one, because it converts a covenant privilege into a charm. The Jerusalem that said it had the temple, the ark’s memory, the Davidic city, and the sacrifices, and it had murdered men in its own streets; and it reasoned that the walls would hold because God’s house stood inside them. Jeremiah met the same slogan — The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, are these (Jer 7:4). The church version is a baptism certificate, a family name, a membership roll, an orthodox confession recited by a heart that has never repented; and the answer is the same. Privilege that is presumed upon becomes the very ground of the sentence: You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you (Amo 3:2).

Recover what the LORD does with their figure, for it is a model of how God answers the self-secure. He does not deny the caldron. He grants it and redefines the contents. There is flesh in the pot — the men you slew; and the security you claimed will be taken from you precisely by being brought out of the walls you trusted, to be judged in the border of Israel where the sword waits. Judgment for such men is not being kept in the pot but being poured out of it. Then hear the mercy that follows in the same chapter, addressed to the despised exiles the princes had written off: Although I have cast them far off among the heathen, yet will I be to them as a little sanctuary in the countries where they shall come (Eze 11:16), and I will give them one heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take the stony heart out of their flesh, and will give them an heart of flesh (Eze 11:19). The men inside the walls had stone hearts and a stone city; the men outside had nothing, and were given a sanctuary and a new heart. Safety was never the masonry. It was the covenant God who makes hearts new.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A great seething pot; Jerusalem’s proverb of false security, turned against her by the LORD.

expand to see more

Caldron — Old French caudron, Latin caldarium, from calidus, hot.

Hebrew sir, a pot or caldron (Eze 11:3); dud, a kettle or basket (1Sa 2:14).

A sanctuary vessel before it was a prophetic figure (2Ch 35:13; Jer 52:18).

The princes’ proverb: walls as the iron pot, themselves as the protected flesh.

The LORD’s reversal: the slain are the flesh, and the secure shall be brought forth to judgment.

Usage

"“It is not near; let us build houses” — the three clauses of carnal security."

"God grants the figure and reverses it: the flesh in the pot is the men you murdered."

"To the exiles outside the walls He promised a little sanctuary and a heart of flesh."
